title: Is Restaurant Delivery Worth It? Here’s How to Work It Out
summary: Does delivery pay off for your restaurant? See real order values from three locations, a simple cost breakdown, and what to check before expanding.
body_markdown:
A $40 delivery order comes in during dinner service. It’s a bigger ticket than many of your counter orders. But once you’ve paid for the food, the packaging and the driver, how much is left?


That’s the question that matters when you’re deciding whether to offer delivery—or do more of it.


We looked at **208 direct delivery orders and 15,568 other orders across three restaurant locations** from May through October 2026. Delivery orders were larger on average. But larger orders alone don’t tell you whether delivery is worth it.


Here’s what we found, and how to use it when looking at your own numbers. This is a small study of three locations, so treat it as a starting point rather than a prediction for your restaurant.


## Delivery orders were bigger. How much bigger?


Delivery orders averaged **$41.48** , compared with **$35.90 for other online orders** . That’s a $5.58 difference, or 15.5%.


These amounts cover food and drinks after discounts and refunds. They leave out tax, tips and delivery or service fees, so the larger tickets weren’t simply the result of adding a delivery charge.


Food-and-drink sales per order at three locations, May–October 2026. All amounts are in US dollars. Order type Orders Average order Middle order*


Direct delivery 208 $41.48 $32.49


Other online orders 1,545 $35.90 $29.98


Other POS orders 14,023 $29.29 $22.98


All non-delivery orders combined 15,568 $29.95 $24.00


**The middle order, or median, is the amount halfway through the orders when you sort them from smallest to largest. Unlike the average, it won’t be pulled up by a handful of very large orders.*


“Other online orders” includes both takeout and orders marked dine-in; it is not a pickup-only group. “Other POS orders” covers the remaining non-delivery orders that weren’t recorded as online payments. It doesn’t tell us exactly where or how each customer ordered. The last row combines those two groups.


Compared with all non-delivery orders, the average delivery ticket was 38.5% larger. But the gap was smaller when we compared delivery with other online orders. That’s a useful reminder: the comparison you choose can change the story.


## Your own restaurant’s numbers matter more than the headline


Imagine combining orders from a sandwich shop and a restaurant selling family dinners. If the family-dinner restaurant supplies most of the delivery orders, the overall delivery average will look higher—even if delivery makes little difference at either restaurant.


We checked for that by comparing order values within each location, then giving all three locations equal weight. The delivery gap fell from 38.5% to **21.6%** against all non-delivery orders, and from 15.5% to just **3.9%** against other online orders.


Comparing delivery and non-delivery within the same location and month gave a 21.1% average gap across 15 qualifying location-and-month comparisons.


The takeaway for your business: compare your delivery orders with similar orders from your own restaurant. A family meal on Saturday night and a solo lunch on Tuesday serve different needs. Menu prices, promotions and what people order can all affect the difference.


## Did delivery customers come back more often?


A bigger order is good. A customer who keeps coming back can be even better. We checked whether customers made another purchase at the same location within 30 days, whether their next order was delivery or something else.


We grouped customers by their **first observed order** during the study. They may already have been regulars before May. We only included customers whose first recorded order was before October 1, giving everyone a full 30 days to return.


Customers with a recorded return purchase within 30 days First recorded order type Customers Came back Return rate


Delivery 72 10 13.9%


Other online orders 809 142 17.6%


Other POS orders 7,831 261 3.3%


Delivery didn’t show a higher return rate than other online orders. With only 72 delivery customers in this comparison, we can’t draw a firm conclusion about which group is more likely to return.


The POS figure needs extra care. We could link 77.5% of regular POS orders to a single customer, compared with all the online orders. Someone could come back, pay without being linked to their earlier purchase, and look like a different customer in the records. **The 3.3% figure is not an estimate of the true in-person customer return rate.**


For your own restaurant, look at both order size and repeat business. Give customers enough time to return, and remember that your reports may miss visits they can’t connect to the same person. Our guide to[measuring restaurant loyalty program ROI](https://avocadopos.com/blog/restaurant-loyalty-program-roi) takes a closer look at comparing customer spending.


## Work out what’s left after each delivery


The sales records tell us what customers spent. They don’t give us the full cost of ingredients, drivers, packaging and extra staff time, so we can’t say how profitable delivery was for these restaurants.


You can work that out for your own business. Start with the food-and-drink sale, add any delivery fee your restaurant actually receives, then subtract the costs of making and delivering the order.


A $40 delivery order: example assumptions, not study results Money in and costs out Example amount


Food-and-drink sale after discounts and refunds $40.00


Delivery fee your restaurant receives, before paying the driver +$3.00


Ingredients −$12.00


Payment and ordering fees −$1.20


Packaging −$1.50


Driver or courier cost −$7.00


Extra staff time −$1.50


Left to cover fixed costs and profit **$19.80**


That $19.80 still needs to help pay rent and other fixed costs before it becomes profit. Accountants call it the order’s *contribution* .


Replace these example amounts with your own costs. Check your payout statements, too: if the driver’s charge has already been deducted from the delivery fee you receive, don’t subtract it again. A delivery fee on the customer’s receipt isn’t necessarily money your restaurant keeps.


If you’re choosing how to handle deliveries, our[guide to third-party and in-house delivery](https://avocadopos.com/blog/third-party-food-delivery-vs-in-house-delivery) walks through the options.


## Are you adding orders, or moving them?


Say delivery brings in ten orders from people who otherwise wouldn’t have bought from you. At the example $19.80 per order, that’s **$198 more to help cover fixed costs and profit** , before any new fixed delivery expenses.


Now imagine those same ten people would have picked up instead. If each pickup order would have left you $20 after its direct costs, switching them to delivery leaves you **$2 worse off** across the ten orders, before any new fixed expenses.


Those are examples, not results from our study. They show why it helps to ask where the orders are coming from. A regular who changes a weekly pickup order to delivery may appreciate the convenience, but you haven’t necessarily gained another sale.


Kitchen space matters here, too. If delivery orders slow down your busiest dinner service, look at what happens to the rest of your business alongside the extra delivery sales.


## Five things to check before you expand delivery


1.


**Compare similar orders.** Look at delivery and other online orders from the same location and service hours. Check whether a few big catering orders or a promotion are lifting the average.


2.


**Add up the full cost.** Include food, packaging, payment fees, the driver and extra staff time. Match the charges to what you actually receive.


3.


**Watch for repeat business.** See who orders again over the next 30 days, including customers who switch between delivery and other ways of ordering.


4.


**Look at the whole restaurant.** Are total sales and the money left after costs improving? Are delivery orders adding work during quiet hours or stretching an already busy kitchen?


5.


**Start with a manageable test.** Try a smaller delivery area or limited hours. Compare similar days and service periods before expanding.


## About the numbers


Avocado reviewed paid orders from May 1 through October 31, 2026, using records available on November 23. Three US locations had enough orders for this comparison: at least 30 direct delivery orders and 100 non-delivery orders each.


We included locations active in Avocado when we ran the study, leaving out test and demo accounts. That means restaurants that had already left the system aren’t represented. We also left out canceled orders, gift-card purchases and orders from third-party marketplaces. Sales are shown after recorded discounts and refunds; later refunds could change the figures.


For repeat purchases, we used orders we could link to one customer and counted a return only on a later day, at the same location, within 30 days. Purchases through other systems or under a different customer record could be missed.


This small study shows what happened at these locations. It doesn’t tell us how much customers would have spent without delivery, or prove that delivery increases sales, loyalty or profit.


To decide whether delivery works for you, start with what each order leaves in your business and whether it brings you additional sales.[Avocado’s ordering and reporting tools](https://avocadopos.com/features) can help you review your orders alongside your own delivery costs.
